title: Multiple Choice Learning of Low-Rank Adapters for Language Modeling
claim: Training K independent low-rank adapters in parallel with a winner-takes-all loss routes stronger gradients only to the best hypothesis.
layout: Single panel, bottom-to-top flow, K parallel columns, gradient arrows in color
description: A single vertical diagram of one linear layer inside a dashed box labeled 'layer ℓ'. A frozen base weight block W_ℓ (blue square) sits at left. Three parallel columns (hypotheses 1, k*, K) each contain pink trapezoid LoRA adapters A (bottom) and B (top), with the winning column k* drawn in a darker shade and thick outlines. Faint gray forward-pass arrows run from the input x at the bottom, through hidden states h^(1), h^(k*), h^(K), through A, B and a ⊕ node that adds the W_ℓ output, then up to p(x|θ_k) and the loss L^WTA at top. Purple backward arrows point down from the loss: thick and dark for the winner, thin and pale for the others. A legend at top left explains the three arrow types.
caption: LoRA-MCL. Components of a linear layer ℓwhere LoRA is enabled, with context c omitted. Frozen base weights Wℓare in blue; trainable LoRA adapters in light red. The forward pass (in gray) is computed independently for each hypothesis, where h(1), . . . , h(K) denote the hidden states as in (34). Gradients (purple arrows) are stronger for the winning hypothesis (k⋆).
abstract: We propose LoRA-MCL, a training scheme that extends next-token prediction in language models with a method designed to decode diverse, plausible sentence continuations at inference time. Traditional language modeling is an intrinsically ill-posed problem: given a context, multiple futures may be equally plausible. Our approach leverages Multiple Choice Learning (MCL) and the winner-takes-all loss to efficiently handle ambiguity through Low-Rank Adaptation. We provide a theoretical interpretation of applying MCL to language modeling, assuming the data is generated from a mixture of distributions. We illustrate the proposed approach using mixtures of Markov chains. We then demonstrate with experiments on audio and visual captioning, as well as machine translation, that our method achieves high diversity and relevance in generated outputs. We release the code for applying LoRA-MCL to a wide range of language models.
